1. Preamble: 
 
Fraud has been a problem for the insurance industry from its early days. Since that time the insurance industry 
has changed considerably. There is an ever-increasing demand to provide excellent service, control claim 
costs, reduce the life cycle of claims and meet policy-holders legitimate expectations. Within the insurance 
market, insurers have to respond quickly, and fairly to policy holders and claimants, which is only right. 
However, it is also imperative that claims are validated properly to ensure that the premium pool which is 
funded by all policy holders is not depleted by the fraudulent activities of the increasing few. 
 
Fraud occurs whenever a suitable opportunity presents itself.  For a business organization it causes avoidable 
financial losses, loss of good will and image and loss of shareholder confidence among others. All well 
managed organizations recognize this reality and take steps to deal with it in a proactive manner.    
                     
IRDAI vide its notification IRDAI/IID/GDL/MISC/112/10/2025 dated 09.10.2025 called upon insurers and 
distribution channels to address and manage risks emerging from frauds. The revised Policy incorporates 
provisions for affinity and complex frauds, alongside regulatory guidelines governing reinsurance-related 
fraud exposures, to ensure regulatory compliance, protection of policyholder interests, and the maintenance 
of high standards of integrity and transparency. Hence, it has been revised in light of these new changes. 
 
Keeping the above guideline in view and the overall approach of National Insurance Company Ltd (Company) 
of following the principles of “Corporate Governance” and implementing “best practices” in all areas 
proactively, it is absolutely necessary that a proper “Anti-Fraud Policy” is formulated, published appropriately 
and implemented in the Company. 
Hence the corporate “Anti- Fraud Policy” (Policy) has been framed, first in 2013, followed by review in 2015, 
2019, 2021, 2022, 2025 and now in FY 2025-26. 
 
2. Scope & Intent: 
 
Any activity with the intention of perpetuating fraud against the Company shall not be tolerated. The sole 
purpose of the policy is to keep on record and provide directions to the Company for prevention, detection, 
mitigation, reporting and remedy of fraud. This would be applicable to all the offices of the Company 
concertedly with related operational guidelines/ instructions issued by the Company from time to time. The 
monitoring and risk management of fraud shall be owned by Chairperson and Managing Directors/Chief 
Executive Officers (CMD/CEOs), Risk Management Committee and Audit Committee of the Board of the 
insurer.  
The Policy is intended to: 
1) Enable understanding of “Fraud” and its implications and effects on the entire organization. 
2) Create a “Fraud Awareness” and “Fraud Prevention” culture in the Company and to send across a 
message within the Company and to the public at large that fraud is not acceptable and shall not be 
tolerated. 
3) Enable prevention and reporting system for pro-active tackling of fraud and make efforts to recover 
fraud losses. 
4) Protect policyholder’s interest, safeguard financial stability and maintain public trust 
5) Encourage Whistle blower complaints  
6) Closer analysis and audit of claims vulnerable to frauds within a specified range in each LOB 
7) Use ML Models with frequent data inputs to identify frauds. 
8) Initiate appropriate action by FMC against the defaulter employee for non-compliance of fraud Risk 
Management Framework.

3. Definition and Common Types of Fraud: 
 
“Fraud”, in general, is a wilful act committed by an individual(s)/ entity(ies) by deception, misrepresentation, 
suppression, cheating or any other fraudulent means or illegal means thereby causing wrongful gain(s) to self 
or any other individual(s) and wrongful loss to the organization. 
In insurance, “Fraud” is an act or omission intended to gain dishonest or unlawful advantage for a party 
committing the fraud or for other related parties. This may for example be caused by means of: 
a) Misappropriating assets 
b) Unauthorized misappropriation of company’s data 
c) Deliberately misrepresenting, concealing, suppressing or not disclosing one or more material facts 
relevant to the financial decision, transaction or perception of the insurer’s status 
d) Abusing responsibility -a position of trust or a fiduciary relationship 
 
The IRDAI circular referred to above recognizes that insurers typically face prospects of fraud of five main 
categories namely  
a) Policyholder Fraud and/or Claims Fraud 
b) Distribution Channel Fraud 
c) Internal Fraud 
d) External Fraud 
e) Affinity Fraud or Complex Fraud 
 
A) Policyholder Fraud and/or Claims Fraud: 
 
Fraud against the Company in the purchase and/or execution of an insurance product including fraud at the 
time of making a claim. These types of frauds include but not limited to:- 
a)   Exaggerating damages/losses 
b)   Staging the occurrence of accidents  
c)   Reporting and claiming fictitious damages/losses 
d)   Medical claims fraud  
e)   Fraudulent death claims 
 
B) Distribution Channel Fraud: 
 
Fraud perpetrated by an insurance agents/ Insurance Brokers/Corporate Agents, bancassurance partner etc. 
against the company and/or policyholders.  
Entities falling under the purview of e-commerce as defined in relevant laws/regulations shall be guided by 
the provisions made under this Policy. 
These types of frauds include but not limited to:- 
a) Premium diversion-Distribution channel takes the premium from the purchaser and does not             
pass it to the insurer 
b) Inflates the premium- Passing on the correct amount to the insurer and keeping the difference  
c) Non-disclosure or misrepresentation of the risk to reduce premium 
 
C) 
Internal Fraud: 
 
Fraud/misappropriation against the Company by its Directors, Managers and/or any other Officers or Staff 
members (by whatever name called). These types of fraud include but not limited to:- 
a)  Misappropriating funds 
b)  Fraudulent financial reporting  
c)  Stealing cheques 
d)  Inflating expenses claims/over-billing  
e)  Forging signatures.

D) 
External Fraud:  
 
External fraud is the risk of unexpected financial, material or reputational loss as the result of fraudulent 
action of persons, external to the National Insurance Company Ltd. External fraud typically refers to frauds 
committed by third parties such as service provider and vendors. These types of frauds include but not limited 
to:- 
a) Premium siphoning and embezzlement 
b) Unauthorized access to insurer’s resources 
c) Inflating repair costs or billing for services not rendered after an insured event 
d) Performing unnecessary medical procedures to bill insurers 
e) Selling fake insurance policies or coverage 
f) Recruitment related fraud 
 
 
E) 
Affinity Fraud or Complex Fraud: Fraud involving collusion among one or more fraud perpetrators 
in the above categories. 
 
4. Cyber or New Age Fraud: 
 
Cyber / New Age Fraud refers to fraudulent activities (such as phishing, hacking, social engineering and such 
methods with intention of unlawful financial gain etc.) that are intended to gain access to personal digital 
information, company sensitive data, stealing/ transferring  monies and or tampering with digital records of 
financial and other assets etc. using digital platforms, technology, or the internet. This type of fraud is 
becoming a significant concern for the insurance sector, as it involves a range of personal and financial 
information that insurers and distribution channels hold about their policyholders/ claimants.  
 
Cyber or New Age Fraud can lead to: 
a) Loss of Confidential Data: Personally identifiable information collected and stored by the company, 
such as KYC details, financial details, and medical records. 
 
b) Sensitive Information being compromised: Insurers may collect sensitive business information such 
as medical records that could be valuable to other corporates / foreign spies/ external entities. In the 
case of certain lines such as cyber insurance products or a kidnap & ransom insurance, the company 
may possess information about a policyholder’s network security controls, head or key executives of 
the client organization in digital form and other cyber resilience information that could be valuable 
and could harm intellectual property rights of either party. 
 
c) Disruption of Operations: Cyber-attacks can result in disruption to normal business operation 
including emails, telephone directories, and voice mails amongst business records such as contract 
templates. 
 
d) Loss of Trust: The foundation of insurance business is policyholder’s trust. Trust that the information 
collected by insurers will be protected, and trust that claims will be paid out in a timely way when 
appropriate. If an insurer were to suffer a cyber-security incident that rendered it unable to make timely 
claims payments that trust may also be shaken. The reputational risk could extend to the sector as a 
whole. 
In order to prevent such frauds, the company shall: 
 
a) 
Cyber Risk Mitigation: - For Prevention of cyber risks, the company shall have in place a 
comprehensive Cyber or New Age Risk Management Policy including SOPs and robust Cybersecurity 
Framework to improve our cybersecurity practices, ensure data protection and ensure compliance with 
regulatory requirements. Overall responsibilities for prevention and taking remedial measures shall lie with 
the CISO. The company shall utilize a team with relevant risk and technological expertise to manage cyber

fraud risks across various insurance business lines. 
 
Company should have comprehensive cyber risk insurance policies, covering first-party and third-party risks. 
This policy should cover damages caused by cyber assaults and costs associated with data recovery, business 
interruption, and legal obligations. 
 
b) 
Creation of Incident Database:  Incident database is a record-keeping system where all fraud-related 
incidents are documented in organization which helps in quick fraud risk identification, detection, prevention 
and mitigation.  
It can be reasonably stated that the company can expect that a fraud could be perpetrated against it by any of 
the following acting alone or in combination with another: 
a) Employee(s), Ex-employee(s) 
b) Persons engaged for work or assignment on temporary/ad-hoc/contract/daily wage basis and/or their 
individual employees/representatives 
c) 
Advisors(s),consultants and similar providers of professional expertise including surveyors/valuers / 
loss adjusters, lawyers, investigators and/ or their individual employees/representatives 
d) Vendors, suppliers of any goods or services to the Company (including IT hardware/software suppliers 
and support and maintenance providers) 
e) Third Party Administrators (TPAs) and/or their individual employees/representatives  
f) Customers/clients of the company and/or their individual employees/representatives  
g) Agents and/or their individual employees/representatives 
h) Brokers and/or their individual employees/representatives. 
i) MISP/ IMFs/ Web Aggregators/ Marketing agencies/ any other intermediary/Service Provider/      
Representatives. 
5. Examples of Fraud: 
 
The following are some of the typical examples of fraud that may be expected. It may be noted that this list 
is merely illustrative and is not exhaustive and it may not be treated as complete for the purpose of this policy: 
a. Willful suppression of facts/deception in matters of appointment, in submission of reports of any nature 
to the company, in any recommendations or making such recommendations as a result of which a 
wrongful gain is made to any person/organization/entity and/or a wrongful loss is caused to the company 
or the public exchequer 
b. Forgery or unauthorized alteration of any document (including certificate of insurance, insurance policy/ 
endorsement/ cover note/ declaration etc.) or correspondence or account belonging to the company 
c. Forgery or unauthorized alteration of cheques, bank drafts or any other financial instruments 
d. Misappropriation of funds, securities, supplies or other assets by fraudulent means 
e. Falsifying records, removing documents/papers/notes from files and/or replacing them 
f. Making fraudulent/false notes in official records of the company 
g. Utilizing company’s funds for the purposes for which the said fund are not intended 
h. Effecting major material deviation from standard laid down tendering procedures or norms without clear 
written authorizations and “speaking orders” 
i. Vendor Fraud (e.g. consideration including the receipt of gifts or accepting or seeking anything from 
contractors, vendors or persons providing services/materials) 
j. Electronic Fraud and/or illegal hacking, unauthorized or illegal manipulation of information technology 
networks or operating systems 
k. Tax evasion 
l. Destruction, removal or inappropriate use of records, furniture, fixtures and equipment of the company 
m. Sales or assignment of fictitious or misrepresented assets

n. Any other act that falls under definition of “Fraud” 
 
6. Internal Reporting of Fraud: 
a) It is the bounden duty of every employee of the company to provide information to the management 
which is within his/her knowledge about any fraud or potential fraud. They will be guided by the 
principle of “Passivity is not an option”. 
b) Every instance of attempted fraud or detected actual fraud (regardless of whether it has caused actual 
financial loss to the company at that juncture or not) shall be reported without delay by the affected 
department/operational unit/any person having knowledge, to the overseeing office/department/ 
executive. Where the fraud involves or is reasonably suspected to involve an employee of the company, 
it shall also be reported to the Vigilance Department at Regional Office (RO) or Head Office (HO) as 
applicable. 
c) Every such instance of fraud shall also be reported to the Fraud Monitoring Committee (FMC) by the 
department/operational unit. 
d) The Board shall encourage anyone having reasonable suspicion to report to appropriate authority and no 
employee shall suffer in any way as a result of reporting reasonably held suspicion. For these purposes 
“reasonably held suspicions” shall mean any suspicions other than those which are shown to be raised 
maliciously and found to be groundless.

7.1.  Constitution of Fraud Monitoring Committee (FMC) and its functions: 
 
 Fraud is a critical risk facing an enterprise that needs to be managed/ controlled/mitigated by the 
Company in an organized way. To achieve this end, a dedicated Fraud Monitoring Committee(FMC) 
as  a  part  of Enterprise  Risk  Management  (ERM)  Department  has  been set  up  in  the company. 
 
 Fraud Monitoring Committee (FMC) shall be headed by the Chief Risk Officer  and also consist of  
Deputy General Manager (DGM) Accounts (Head office) & Officers preferably of the rank of Scale 
V from concerned Line of Business(LOB) /Departments at Head Office.  
 
 The FMC may establish sub-committees or task forces for its effective functioning.  
 
 FMC shall meet once in a quarter (or as and when required) to discuss the matters relating to Fraud 
Prevention and monitoring. 
 
     The function of FMC is to:  
a) Recommend and regularly update, based on experiences, appropriate measures on fraud risk 
management to various functions. 
b) Oversee prompt responses to instances or suspicions of fraud. 
c) Maintain all relevant details pertaining to each instance of fraud. 
d) Facilitate collaboration with industry peers / bodies, law enforcement agencies and regulatory bodies 
to pursue cases of fraud and share information / intelligence on known fraud schemes and perpetrators. 
e) Conduct an Annual Comprehensive Fraud Risk Assessment to identify potential vulnerabilities across 
business lines and activities for fraud, using past experiences, emerging trends & Red Flag Indicators 
(RFIs), etc. 
f) Identify areas for improvement and adaptation of the Fraud Risk Management Framework. 
g) Submit report of the Annual Comprehensive Fraud Risk Assessment before RMC through CRO, 
based on the data of fraud reported. 
 
7.2. Fraud Monitoring Unit (FMU): 
 
Nodal officers and Regional In-charges at their respective ROs and CBOs level along with senior Accounts 
Official at the respective ROs/hubs and CBOs level, shall constitute an independent Fraud Monitoring Unit 
(FMU), separate from internal audit, which will support FMC in discharging its functions and shall be 
responsible for implementing measures for fraud deterrence, prevention, detection, monitoring, investigation, 
reporting and providing remedy at their respective ROs and CBOs level.  
The functions of the FMU, in addition to supporting FMC, shall inter alia include:  
 
a) Effective implementation of measures suggested by FMC. 
b) Monitoring insurance claims, policy applications, and verifying transactions as well as information 
through RFIs (Red Flag Indicators) and detailed investigations. 
c) Investigations along with evidence gathering and collaboration with relevant departments, ensuring 
conflicts of interest are identified and avoided. 
d) Timely reporting of identified fraud cases to FMC and maintaining transactional-wise details of each 
and every fraud including action taken. 
e) Coordinate with industry peers/bodies, law enforcement agencies (LEAs) and regulatory bodies to 
pursue cases of fraud and share information/intelligence on known fraud schemes and perpetrators. 
 
7.3.  Nomination of Nodal Officer and Role: 
 A senior level officer, preferably Scale IV, is nominated at each RO to receive information from various 
operating offices and take necessary action. The Nodal Officers should report to the FMC at Head 
Office of the company.

 The FMU shall implement the modules suggested by FMC to create awareness among the employees 
and officers in fraud detection and mitigation. 
 The awareness modules suggested by the FMC for employees and officers including distribution 
channel, service providers & intermediaries   in fraud detection and mitigation shall be implemented 
by the Nodal Officers in their respective ROs/CBOs and by the ERM Department at the Head Office.  
 Nodal Officer to coordinate with Operating Offices under its jurisdiction for implementing SOPs and 
reporting of frauds and maintaining data repository for fraud claims. 
 Any outsider(s) or employee(s) who is in the knowledge or come across any fraud/ fraudulent practices 
committed by an intermediary or policyholder or employee can notify the same to Nodal Officer at 
RO/CBO or FMC at HO directly, if he/she deems it necessary. If the issue has already been investigated 
by the operating offices, then such investigation report shall also be forwarded to the Nodal Officer of 
the respective RO/CBO.  
 The Nodal Officer of the respective RO/CBO is authorized to take original records from operating 
offices/ take copies/ emails or any other communication as he may decide to be required for the purpose 
of establishing the fraud committed. 
 The Nodal Officer in concurrence with FMU at their respective RO/CBO, with the assistance of 
involved operating office, is authorized to initiate action by law enforcing agencies including the police 
authorities against the persons who have been identified to have committed the fraud. 
 
7.4. Organizational Structure: 
 
 The FMU shall report to the FMC on a monthly basis, providing details of all fraud cases reported and 
pending within the respective offices. In the event that no fraud cases are reported during a month, a 
‘Nil’ report must be submitted.(point included for importance of reporting fraud on monthly basis) 
 FMC should submit quarterly detailed reports of fraud cases to Risk Management Committee (RMC) 
of the Board. It shall also report to Audit Committee and RMC in case of Internal Fraud. 
 RMC will suggest corrective measures to FMC for eliminating fraud and it may further consult for 
corrective measures or may seek advice  from  GM IT, Chief Compliance Officer, GM Audit, ERM 
Department Head Office, Chief Financial Officer (CFO) or any other officer, as and when required, 
based on the nature of Frauds. 
 RMC should review the reports submitted by FMC, recommend system checks and alert the Audit and 
Vigilance Department. 
 FMC in turn will suggest mitigation steps to the Fraud Monitoring Unit (FMU), in line with the 
corrective measures suggested by RMC that is to be implemented and documented. 
 
8. Fraud Risk Management Framework 
 
The Company shall maintain a robust Fraud Risk Management Framework (FRMF) designed to proactively 
identify, assess, mitigate, and monitor fraud risks across all business functions. The Risk Management 
Committee (RMC) shall be responsible for effective implementation and oversight of the fraud risk 
management framework. The framework is built upon the principle of Zero Tolerance toward fraud. The 
fraud risk management framework shall be specific to the insurer’s business considering the nature of 
business, size, risk profile, overall business strategy, products, distributions channels, technology 
infrastructure, and any other applicable parameter including various activities. The IRDA in its 2025 
Regulation has mentioned five categories of fraud as a result the Fraud Risk Management Framework has 
been modified to include this classification:

8.1. Mechanism to deal with Internal Fraud: 
 
a) The Company has also an Internal Audit and Inspection Department (IA &ID) that audits transactions and 
accounts which on occasion reveal commission of frauds. 
b) The Company already has a well-defined system and procedure for tackling internal frauds i.e. frauds 
committed by company’s own employees, through the Vigilance Department. The Vigilance Department 
itself has the avowed intent to be proactive in implementing “Preventive Vigilance” by means of making 
system studies, anticipating fraud prone areas, spreading awareness and sensitizing drives, conducting 
surprise checks and so on. It is also expressly tasked with investigation of suspected frauds by own 
employees acting by themselves or in concert with outside elements and bringing established cases of 
fraud (with evidence) to suitable conclusion by disciplinary proceedings or any other appropriate punitive 
measure. The Department functions in the light of the Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules (CDA 
Rules). 
c) The function or intent of the Fraud Monitoring Committee (FMC) is not to take over, duplicate or even 
overlap the functions of these two departments but to act in co-ordination with them. By itself, the FMC 
shall also pay particular attention to studying and monitoring fraud emanating from policy 
holders/customers as well as from intermediaries. The FMC shall: 
 
I. 
Co-operate actively with the Vigilance, and IA &ID departments to respond to fraud allegations 
II. 
Collect fraud data from these departments and from the operational units of the Company 
III. 
Analyze these 
IV. 
Identify Risk Indicators 
V. 
Suggest effective control mechanism  
VI. 
Report periodically to the Risk Management Committee of the Board 
d) However, in cases of frauds involving more than one entity, one of which is an internal entity, the SOP 
shall be as per the Affinity or Complex Fraud. 
 
8.2. SOP for alleged frauds by Policyholders/ Claimants 
 
STEP 1: Recording                                                
 
                 Timeline: Immediate 
The Fraud needs to be recorded by the Office. This would include details obtained, source from which 
information received, documents received thereof, and other material facts.  
 
STEP 2:  Internal Verification                                                                    Timeline: Initiation within 3 days 
Based on information and documents above, to ascertain whether it is policy-related or claim related. Office 
to verify the existence of policy, declarations in proposals, whether any mis-declaration /suppression of 
material information has been resorted to in commission of the fraud. Also if claim related, whether reported, 
it’s present status etc. It should be initiated within 3 days of receiving the complaint.  
 
STEP 3: Investigation                                                                Timeline: Report submission within 15 days 
Decide on Investigation agency, whether by Office, or through professional investigator. Specify terms of 
reference under which investigation is to be carried out. Timeline for report submission should be as early as 
possible but maximum 15 days, unless there are extenuating circumstances for delay, which should be 
recorded. Report should highlight whether any collusion exists between Insured and other entities.

STEP 4: Action on finding               
           Timeline: Within 30 days of receipt of report 
If found established, action to be taken against the policyholder. Action would involve cancellation of policy

STEP 5: Reporting by Offices         Timeline: Immediate to Nodal Officer, and Monthly on given template 
Offices to intimate frauds to Nodal Officer as and when they occur, and to keep Nodal Officer informed at all

be done on a standard template. 
 
STEP 6: Reporting by Nodal Officer                                         Timeline: by 7th of every succeeding month

STEP 7: Review and action by FMC                                             Timeline: meeting every month 
FMC shall review the reports submitted by each Nodal Officer for the month. They will also examine the 
action taken at the ground level (Operating Office/RO), and decide on whether further action, other than those 
initiated, need to be taken. 
STEP 8:  Reporting to RMC and Internal Audit Committee  
 
          Timeline: Quarterly basis 
FMC to collate the reports and summarize each of the cases for information to the Risk Management 
Committee and Internal Audit Committee through the CRO. 
 
ERM Review: 
The directions of the RMC/Board to be recorded for compliance, and report thereof on Action Taken, to be 
placed before the RMC in subsequent meeting(s). 
All the frauds (other than internal frauds), reported to HO, need to be analyzed by the ERM Team, with the 
assistance of the FMC. Necessary checks to prevent occurrences are to be identified, and put in place. As a 
part of information sharing, details of established fraudsters/ repeated offenders to be shared on Fraud 
Monitoring Portal of GI Council and also to all our offices. Recommended system checks to be intimated to 
IT for building into the program. The Audit and Vigilance Departments shall be alerted to conduct inspections 
/ special audits to verify/ ascertain the veracity of the fraud allegations

8.3. SOP For Frauds by Distribution Channels  (individual Agents, Corporate Agents, Brokers, 
POS, IMF, Web Aggregators etc.): 
 
STEP 1: Identification & Recording                                                                                   Timeline: Immediate 
Identify the entity allegedly having committed fraud and this is to be recorded by the Office. This would 
include details obtained, source from which information received, documents received thereof, and other 
material facts. 
STEP 2:  Internal Verification                      
     Timeline: Initiation within 3 days 
Verify the stage at which alleged fraud has been initiated. Prima facie involvement of agent / broker / 
intermediary would require review of their portfolio within 3 days, so this needs to be flagged, pending final 
investigation. Prima facie involvement of surveyor / advocate / service provider would require suspension of 
work, pending final investigation. 
STEP 3: Investigation                                                             Timeline: Report Submission within 15 days 
Decide who shall conduct the investigation whether by Office, or through professional investigator. Specify 
terms of reference under which investigation is to be carried out. Timeline for report submission should be as 
early as possible but maximum 15 days, unless there are extenuating circumstances for delay, which should 
be recorded. Report should highlight whether any collusion between Intermediary and other entities. 
STEP 4: Action on Finding 
            Timeline: Within 30 days of receipt of report 
If fraud is found established, action to be taken against the Intermediary would involve the following, which 
is indicative, and not exhaustive: 
a) For Individual Agents: Depending on nature and severity of offence, the Operating Office can 
recommend suggested action to the FMU. This could involve suspension/ temporary blocking of 
business code as per terms of the contract. Information should be disseminated to all our offices also 
so that the agent is not entertained elsewhere. HO Marketing to be kept abreast of action taken against 
individual Agents. 
 
The concerned Technical department at HO shall, then act immediately as per the directives of this Committee. 
b) For Brokers/Corporate Agents/Other Intermediaries: The process will be similar to (ii) above. The 
Committee in this case will include DGM (Marketing) also. The Committee shall decide on the action 
to be taken, both at Company level and for reporting to IRDAI. 
 
 
STEPS 5, 6, 7 (Reporting Procedure), and ERM REVIEW: 
Similar to what has been outlined in SOP for Policy Holder Fraud mentioned above. 
8.4 SOP for Cyber Fraud: 
STEP 1: Recording                                                
 
                 Timeline: Immediate 
Any attempt of or suspected of hacking, phishing or unauthorized access to data/ computer resources shall be 
reported to HOIT Security team immediately/ as soon as it comes to the notice of any employee. Any 
attempted/ actual cyber frauds reported to Nodal Officers shall be forwarded to the HOIT Security Team

derived by dividing the Inherent Risk Score (IR) with Overall Control Score (C). This score can be aggregated at a process/ business/ company level for the purpose of
